docs.title: FLEX (computed)
docs.text: FLEX droplet burns: 186 of 276 tests ended in visible-flame extinction, 62 in disruption and 28 burned to completion.
docs.source_ref: NASA/TP-2015-216046, Table IX (computed from the CSV)

docs.title: FLEX (computed)
docs.text: Methanol droplets extinguished in 126 of 157 tests (80.3%); n-heptane droplets in 60 of 119 (50.4%). Fuel chemistry matters as much as atmosphere.
docs.source_ref: NASA/TP-2015-216046, Table IX (computed from the CSV)

docs.title: FLEX (computed)
docs.text: Cool flames, invisible burning: of 60 n-heptane tests logged as Extinction, 39 show evidence of cool-flame burning after the visible flame went out, 8 show none, 6 are unclear.

docs.title: FLEX (computed)
docs.text: Dilution of the atmosphere: carbon dioxide was present in 123 FLEX tests (up to 0.70 mole fraction) and helium in 51 (up to 0.45). CO2 and helium were never combined in one test.
docs.source_ref: NASA/TP-2015-216046, Table IX (computed from the CSV)

docs.title: FLEX (computed)
docs.text: FLEX tested ambient oxygen from 12% to 34% and pressure from 0.69 to 3.05 atm, all in still gas and microgravity.
docs.source_ref: NASA/TP-2015-216046, Table IX (computed from the CSV)

docs.title: FLEX (computed)
docs.text: Methanol with CO2 in the atmosphere: 61 of 75 tests ended in extinction (81%); with nitrogen only: 39 of 54 (72%). Other conditions differ between the groups.
docs.source_ref: NASA/TP-2015-216046, Table IX (computed from the CSV)

docs.title: FLEX (computed)
docs.text: Heptane with CO2 in the atmosphere: 27 of 48 tests ended in extinction (56%); with nitrogen only: 19 of 48 (40%). Other conditions differ between the groups.
docs.source_ref: NASA/TP-2015-216046, Table IX (computed from the CSV)

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: Glovebox oxygen was varied from 13.6% to 22.2% by volume across the BASS-II tests; PSI's experimental table lists 129 tests in that range.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: The flow duct produced 0 to 55 cm/s; about 55 cm/s was the maximum with no flow restrictor fitted.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: For PMMA rods in concurrent (stagnation) flow the microgravity flammability boundary has its minimum at about 13.5% O2, against an upward flame-spread limit of 15.4% O2 in normal gravity.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: In one quenching test on a PMMA rod of 0.476 cm radius, oxygen was set to 14.8% at the start and read 13.6% at the end, with the flame still present before quenching.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: The investigators report steady spreading at 13.6% O2 in microgravity where the normal-gravity blowoff limit for the same quarter-inch PMMA rod is 16% O2: a negative oxygen margin of 2.4% O2.
docs.source_ref: Ferkul et al., BASS-II poster, ASGSR 2014, slide 18 (NTRS 20160000593)

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: For black PMMA rods in opposed flow, flame spread was seen down to 17.5% O2 in microgravity but not below 19% in normal gravity.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: Heat release rates, estimated from oxygen consumption at 13.1 kJ per gram of O2, were well below 100 W for most tests.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: The global equivalence ratio was estimated as fuel rich, 1.3 on average.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: SIBAL fabric (2.2 cm wide) in concurrent flow quenched when the flow was stepped down to 2.2 cm/s at 18.7% O2, 2.2 cm/s at 17.5%, 2.6 cm/s at 17.4% and 2.8 cm/s at 16.9%.
docs.source_ref: NASA/TM-20210011385 Table 7.1 (report p. 96), tests GMT45-T4, GMT100-T13, GMT175-T18, GMT178-T14

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: One 1.2-cm SIBAL sample blew off when flow was raised to 47 cm/s at 17.2% O2; a 2.2-cm sample did not blow off at 53 cm/s at 16.9% O2.
docs.source_ref: NASA/TM-20210011385 Table 7.1 (report p. 96), tests GMT190-T21 and GMT178-T17

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: SIBAL fabric did not ignite at 16.4% O2 (flows of 5 and 10 cm/s) or at 16.8% O2 (5 cm/s).
docs.source_ref: NASA/TM-20210011385 Table 7.1 (report p. 96), tests GMT175-T9, GMT175-T10, GMT178-T12

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: PMMA slabs 1 to 5 mm thick burned for 6.4 to 30.7 minutes with spread rates of 0.012 to 0.144 mm/s at 17.9 to 22.2% initial O2.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: Thin PMMA film: critical flow velocity for steady spread about 1 cm/s in air; blowoff at 28 cm/s (17.3% O2) and 33 cm/s (17.4% O2); no blowoff at 45 cm/s in 21% O2.
docs.source_ref: Olson, Ferkul et al., ICES-2019-101 §III.A, as reported in the research notes

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: CO yield 0.014 to 0.14 g CO per g MMA, up to ten times normal-gravity PMMA values.
docs.source_ref: ICES-2019-101 §III, as reported in the research notes

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: Concurrent rods produced on average 550 ppm of CO for every 1% of CO2 and thick slabs 370 ppm; efficient flue gas is about ten times cleaner.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: Flames extinguished when the flow was turned off in every BASS-II test where it was tried; critical velocity for thin fuels 1 to 5 cm/s.
docs.source_ref: ICES-2019-101 §IV, as reported in the research notes

docs.title: BASS
docs.text: BASS consists of 41 fuel samples burned for a total of 89 test points; BASS-II consists of 100 fuel samples.

docs.title: SoFIE-GEL
docs.text: Extinction limits of 4-cm PMMA spheres were mapped over forced flows of 0.2 to 80 cm/s, 13 to 34% O2 and 0.15 to 1.1 atm; the minimum oxygen is slightly below 14% and the quenching and blowoff branches merge at a strain rate of 7.5 per second.
docs.source_ref: T'ien et al., Combust. Flame 277 (2025) 114244, abstract and conclusions

docs.title: SoFIE-GEL
docs.text: Five tabulated extinctions of 4-cm PMMA spheres at 1.03 to 1.07 atm: quench at 4.83 cm/s and 14.21% O2; blowoff at 34.28 cm/s and 14.99%; intermediate at 11.50 cm/s and 13.54%; quench at 0.44 cm/s and 20.77%; blowoff at 49.68 cm/s and 14.37%.
docs.source_ref: Li, T'ien, Ferkul, Olson, 40th Int. Symp. Combust. paper, Table 1 (NTRS 20240007628)

docs.title: SAME
docs.text: SAME (first flight) geometric mean smoke particle diameters, unaged: Kapton 80 nm, Teflon 170 nm, lamp wick 186 nm, silicone rubber 189 nm. After 720 s of ageing: 155, 228, 258 and 352 nm.
docs.source_ref: Urban et al., SAME Final Report (NIST, 5 Mar 2010), Table 1

docs.title: SAME
docs.text: A substantial portion of the smoke particles from overheated spacecraft materials are below 500 nm in diameter.

docs.title: SAME
docs.text: Mixing dominates smoke transport in microgravity, so detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity. The report gives no lag in seconds; smoke was aged 10 to 1800 s to simulate transport.

docs.title: SAME
docs.text: The station-type smoke detector failed to alarm for Kapton smoke in half of the tests and for Teflon smoke in two-thirds of the tests.
docs.source_ref: Fire-detection white paper for the 2023-2032 Decadal Survey, p. 2 (summarising SAME results)

docs.title: SAME-R
docs.text: SAME-R (reflight) geometric mean diameters, unaged to aged 720 s: Kapton 42 to 89 nm; lamp wick 90 to 229 nm; silicone 128 to 269 nm; Teflon 81 to 70 nm; Pyrell 149 to 293 nm. Repeatability about 15%.

docs.title: SAME
docs.text: A well-mixed vehicle model gives the mass of cellulose that must pyrolyse before an alarm: 7.9 g for a 53 m3 station module (10 mg/m3 threshold), 1.0 g for a 37 m3 shuttle cabin (2 mg/m3), 0.9 g for a 6 m3 capsule (10 mg/m3). These are masses, not times.

docs.title: Saffire-I
docs.text: Steady concurrent spread rates over thin fabric: Saffire I SIBAL 0.18 cm/s (20 cm/s flow, 21.7% O2, 102 kPa); Saffire III SIBAL 0.23 cm/s (25 cm/s, 21.2%, 99 kPa); Saffire IV SIBAL 0.36 cm/s; Saffire V cotton 0.34 cm/s.
docs.source_ref: Olson et al., Combust. Flame 248 (2023) 112559, Table 1 (author accepted manuscript)

docs.title: Saffire-VI
docs.text: Test atmospheres: IV-1 SIBAL 100.0 kPa, 22.0% O2; V-2 cotton jersey 70.7 kPa, 26.2%; VI-2 SIBAL 54.1 kPa, 31.0%; VI-3 two-sided PMMA 54.6 kPa, 30.3%; VI-4 one-sided PMMA 55.2 kPa, 28.8%. All at 20 cm/s; free volume 16.7 to 19.0 m3.

docs.title: Saffire-VI
docs.text: Peak heat release by oxygen-consumption calorimetry: VI-2 SIBAL 3,217 W (580 kJ total, 112 s burn); VI-3 two-sided PMMA 3,080 W (1,280 kJ, 780 s); VI-4 one-sided PMMA 1,507 W (830 kJ, 1,200 s). No oxygen-calorimetry values exist for Saffire IV or V.

docs.title: Saffire-IV
docs.text: Average heat release by fuel-consumption calorimetry: IV-1 SIBAL 3,150 W (409 kJ, 130 s burn); V-2 cotton jersey 2,800 W (560 kJ, 200 s); VI-2 SIBAL 3,650 W (409 kJ). These are averages, not peaks.

docs.title: Saffire-VI
docs.text: Far-field CO2 partial pressure rose by 3.51 mmHg (VI-3) and 3.37 mmHg (VI-4), above the 3 mmHg one-hour limit; far-field CO rose by 308 and 320 ppm against a one-hour limit of 425 ppm and a 24-hour limit of 100 ppm.

docs.title: Saffire-VI
docs.text: In VI-3 (two-sided PMMA, 30.3% O2, 54.6 kPa) the far-field detector reached a 1 mg/m3 alarm threshold at 981 s, after much of the hazardous gas had been released. This is an absolute microgravity time, not a comparison with normal gravity.

docs.title: Saffire-VI
docs.text: A 2026 paper tabulates thin-fuel spread rates side by side: IV-1 SIBAL 3.6 mm/s at 980 mbar, V-2 cotton 3.4 mm/s at 741 mbar, VI-2 SIBAL 4.05 mm/s at 541 mbar. Thick PMMA did not spread; its flame length grew at 0.22 to 0.38 mm/s.

docs.title: Saffire-VI
docs.text: Time to a 2 mg/m3 aerosol alarm at the far-field detector: thin fuels 92 s (IV-1), 146 s (V-2), 201 s (VI-2); thick PMMA 1,083 s (IV-2), 1,117 s (V-3), 1,037 s (VI-3), 1,603 s (VI-4). The table does not state time zero, and PMMA samples were preheated for about ten minutes.

docs.title: Saffire-VI
docs.text: The 2026 paper gives Saffire VI peak heat release as 3,376 W (VI-2), 3,240 W (VI-3) and 1,487 W (VI-4), slightly different from the 2024 paper's 3,217, 3,080 and 1,507 W. Both are shown; neither is averaged.
docs.source_ref: ICES-2026-577, Table 1, compared with ICES-2024-365, Table 2

docs.title: Saffire-IV
docs.text: Two-colour pyrometry of the Saffire IV SIBAL flame gives an average soot temperature of about 1300 K (1305 K in the body) with an uncertainty of 117 K, roughly constant during spread.
docs.source_ref: Thomsen et al., Proc. Combust. Inst. 39 (2023) 3909-3918, accepted manuscript (NTRS 20220012861)

docs.title: Saffire-VI
docs.text: Saffire VI started at 54.1 kPa and 31.0% O2, an oxygen partial pressure of about 16.8 kPa. That is lower than sea-level air (21.2 kPa) even though the oxygen fraction is higher.
docs.source_ref: Niehaus et al., ICES-2025-156, p. 3 (NTRS 20250002675); partial pressure computed here

docs.title: Saffire-I
docs.text: PSI's table for Saffire-I lists two SIBAL samples, 40.6 by 94 cm, at 20 cm/s: a concurrent burn of 420 s at 21.5 to 21.7% O2 and an opposed burn of 70 s at about 21.5% O2.

docs.title: ACME-BRE
docs.text: On a 25-mm burner emulating condensed fuels in still gas, every flame in 21% O2 self-extinguished within 40 s; steady flames were observed at 26.5%, 34% and 40% O2.
docs.source_ref: Dehghani, PhD thesis, Univ. of Maryland 2022, abstract

docs.title: ACME-BRE
docs.text: Emulated-material flames in still gas self-extinguish at oxygen concentrations below about 25% by volume.
docs.source_ref: Stocker et al., ACME overview, JASMAC-33 (2021), slide 4 (NTRS 20210022542)

docs.title: ACME-BRE
docs.text: Of 103 flames at 21, 26.5, 34 and 40% O2, 49 burned until the fuel was shut off. A critical steady flame temperature of 1100 to 1200 K separates sustained from self-extinguished flames.

docs.title: ACME-BRE
docs.text: PSI's BRE table lists test days at nominal oxygen concentrations of 21, 26.5, 34 and 40%; chamber pressure was also varied but is not given in the table.

docs.title: ACME-CLD
docs.text: Sooty microgravity coflow flames are taller and wider and contain 5 to 8 times more soot than equivalent normal-gravity flames. No numeric extinction or dilution limit table has been published openly.

docs.title: ACME-sFlame
docs.text: Spherical flames: radiative extinction seems to occur at high flow rates and kinetic extinction at low flow rates; with helium dilution the limits shift. Reported qualitatively only.

docs.title: ACME-CFI-G
docs.text: PSI's CFI-G normal-flame table marks 7 of 179 tests as cool flames: all 30% n-butane fuel, chamber oxygen mole fraction 0.39 to 0.40, about 2.03 bar. Five are on day 174 of 2021 and two on day 291.
docs.source_ref: PSI-159 experimental table, normal flames, column 'Cool flame?'

docs.title: ACME-CFI-G
docs.text: After more than 150 hot flames, three cool flames were first noticed on 23 June 2021: n-butane diluted with nitrogen, 40% O2 in nitrogen, 2 atm. Cool flames burn at 600 to 1000 K against 1100 to 2200 K for hot flames.
docs.source_ref: University of Maryland Fire Protection Engineering news release, 2021

docs.title: ACME-CFI-G
docs.text: 85% O2 is an inverse-flame burner feed, not a cabin-like ambient. In inverse (inside-out) flames the chamber holds fuel and the oxygen stream comes out of the burner. PSI's inverse-flame tables for CFI-G and for Flame Design both reach a burner oxygen mole fraction of 0.85; chamber-ambient oxygen in the normal-flame tables never exceeds 0.40.
docs.source_ref: PSI-159 and PSI-10 experimental tables (inverse flames, column XO2); Frolov et al., Fire 6 (2023) 285, Table 2

docs.title: ACME-FlameDesign
docs.text: Spherical ethylene diffusion flames at atmospheric pressure burned for 28 to 336 s; larger flames went out by radiative extinction.
docs.source_ref: Irace et al., Combust. Flame 229 (2021) 111373, abstract

docs.title: ACME-FlameDesign
docs.text: PSI's Flame Design normal-flame table (207 tests) has chamber oxygen mole fractions from 0.198 to 0.400.
docs.source_ref: PSI-10 experimental table, normal flames, column 'XO2 (init)'

docs.title: ACME-EFIELD
docs.text: E-FIELD Flames used electric fields to push on flame ions. The challenge brief describes this as mimicking partial gravity; no source gives a calibration from field strength to a gravity level.
docs.source_ref: Official challenge brief; Stocker et al., JASMAC-33 paper, Table 2 (operations March to May and September to November 2018)

docs.title: ACME-CLD
docs.text: Across the six ACME experiments more than 1,500 flames were ignited, over three times the number planned.

docs.title: FLEX
docs.text: For oxygen/nitrogen mixtures the limiting oxygen index of the droplets is reported as 0.12 for methanol and 0.15 for n-heptane.
docs.source_ref: Dietrich et al., Microgravity Sci. Technol. 26 (2014) 65-76, abstract

docs.title: FLEX-2
docs.text: Measured burning-rate constants, hot flame then cool flame, mm2/s: n-decane at 0.5 atm 0.41 / 0.33 (21% O2), 0.31 / 0.27 (17%), 0.29 / 0.25 (14%); n-octane at 1 atm and 21% O2 0.48 / 0.38 in nitrogen, 0.54 / 0.43 with 15% helium, 0.63 / 0.53 with 50% helium. No such table for n-heptane was found openly, and no single K exists for any fuel.

docs.title: FLEX
docs.text: An open six-step cool-flame model for n-heptane gives activation temperatures of 19,840 K, 12,090 K and 15,110 K for its three decomposition steps and predicts a cool-flame limiting oxygen mole fraction on the order of 0.1. The one-step parameters fitted in 2012 are not available openly.
docs.source_ref: Williams and Nayagam, Combust. Theory Model. 23(4) (2019) 748-770, Table 1 (open copy)

docs.title: FLEX
docs.text: Cool-flame standoff ratio: numerical results vary between 2.6 and 3.3, quasi-steady theory gives 3.1, and a measured value of 3.2 is reported for n-decane in air.
docs.source_ref: Nayagam, Dietrich and Williams, ASGSR 2015 slides 11-12 (NTRS 20160000344)

docs.title: LUCI
docs.text: LUCI, simulated lunar gravity on a spinning suborbital capsule, air at normal pressure: SIBAL fabric burning downward spread at 0.92 mm/s (flame base) against 1.5 mm/s in normal gravity, and its flame lasted about 45 s longer than the normal-gravity burn.
docs.source_ref: Ferkul et al., ASGSR 2025 presentation, slides 19, 33, 34 (NTRS 20250010653)

docs.title: LUCI
docs.text: LUCI, 4-mm PMMA rod burning upward: flame tip spread at 0.15 cm/s in simulated lunar gravity against 0.40 cm/s in normal gravity; chamber oxygen fell from 20% to 14.3% during the burn. The base did not reach steady spread and no limiting oxygen value is stated.

docs.title: LUCI
docs.text: LUCI created lunar gravity by rotating the vehicle at 11 RPM with a 1.22 m effective radius, for a burn of about two and a half minutes. Coriolis force affects the flames. It is one flight, in air, with two samples sharing one chamber.

docs.title: Lunar-g drop-tower centrifuge
docs.text: Drop-tower centrifuge tests at 8.2 psia on five materials give a worst-case difference of 2.3% O2 between normal-gravity and lunar-gravity flammability limits. Polycarbonate and Nomex Velcro went out at higher oxygen in lunar gravity than the normal-gravity data. Test time is 5.2 s.
docs.source_ref: Urban et al., ICES-2025-392, Table 2 text (NTRS 20250002114)

docs.title: Lunar-g drop-tower centrifuge
docs.text: The buoyant flow speed that controls a flame in lunar gravity is not established: a 2025 paper takes 35 cm/s as a high estimate for normal gravity and calls the lunar value not known; a 2004 paper expects more than 20 cm/s on the Moon and Mars.

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text: An earlier scaling estimate puts buoyant flow at 24 cm/s in normal gravity, about 10 cm/s in lunar gravity and about 15 cm/s in Martian gravity.
docs.source_ref: ICES-2019-101 §III.F, as reported in the research notes

docs.title: KC-135 partial-gravity flights
docs.text: Thin cellulose burning upward in air at 0.2 to 0.4 atm on parabolic flights at 0.1 g, 0.16 g, 0.38 g and 1 g: steady spread speed and pyrolysis length were roughly proportional to gravity. About 25 s per parabola.

docs.title: Parabolic-flight wire tests
docs.text: Insulated wires on parabolic flights (0, 0.16, 0.38, 1 g): spread rate rises steadily with gravity for copper cores, but shows a peak at low gravity for nickel-chromium cores, in the paper's body limited to two samples at low oxygen.
docs.source_ref: Konno et al., Proc. Combust. Inst. 39 (2023) 3785-3794, author manuscript

docs.title: FM2
docs.text: The FM2 team's motivation: earlier numerical and experimental work suggests flame spread rate peaks, and the oxygen needed for flammability reaches a minimum, near lunar gravity.

docs.title: FM2
docs.text: FM2 is planned, not flown. Flight Unit 1: four 20-cm samples of a crew-clothing fabric burning upward at 37, 33, 29 and 25% O2, all at 8.2 psia, in a 14.7 L chamber delivered by an uncrewed lander demonstration. The newest source gives no launch date.
docs.source_ref: Ferkul et al., presentation to the National Academies, 29 Sep 2026, slides 8-9

docs.title: Challenge brief
docs.text: Spacesuits are filled with 100% oxygen at 4.3 psi; the atmosphere used on the Moon will likely be 30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less.
docs.source_ref: Official challenge brief, Flame in Freefall

docs.title: Challenge brief
docs.text: The PSI repository currently holds no partial-gravity combustion data.
docs.source_ref: Official challenge brief, Flame in Freefall

docs.title: FLEX
docs.text: Flame Extinguishment Experiment The FLEX (Flame Extinguishment Experiment) investigation aims to map the flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity environments, measure the effectiveness of various gaseous fire suppressants such as CO2, He, and SF6, and develop reliable predictive models for combustion limits under reduced gravity conditions. The mission seeks to validate and improve simplified models by incorporating detailed chemical reactions, heat transfer, and material movement, using both space-based data and extensive ground-based tests. Key flight experiment goals include obtaining high-resolution measurements of droplet burning rates, flame extinction behavior, heat radiation, soot levels, and temperature profiles, while systematically analyzing the effects of different ambient conditions and suppressant concentrations. These investigations are essential for advancing the fundamental understanding of combustion processes in microgravity and enhancing fire safety protocols for future space missions. methanol; n-heptane single droplet, 1.10 to 4.67 mm initial diameter Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)-Fluids and Combustion Facility (FCF), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA)
docs.source_ref: NASA/TP-2015-216046, Table IX and Appendix B captions

docs.title: FLEX-2
docs.text:
Flame Extinguishment Experiment - 2 The primary goal of the FLEX-2 flight experiments is to extend the results of FLEX-1 to fuels and environmental conditions that mimic real combustor conditions, as well as, provide benchmark experimental data on bi-component droplet combustion over a wide range of initial conditions in order to validate numerical simulations and to develop new theoretical models.

Detailed experimental objectives can be further itemized as:
  1. Investigate the role of liquid-phase mixing on the burning characteristics of bi-component fuel droplets.
  2. Examine the steady and unsteady liquid and gas-phase phenomena in pure fuel combustion.
  3. Study flame extinction mechanisms and their boundaries.
  4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics.
  5. Determine the influence of droplet interactions on the flammability limits and extinction behavior of droplet arrays.
  6. Validate theoretical models of droplet combustion through comprehensive experimental data collection in microgravity environments. iso-octane; n-octane; heptane; decane; ethanol; mixtures single droplet, 1.5 to 5 mm (PSI test matrix) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Multi-user Droplet Combustion Appartatus (MDCA)

docs.title: CFI
docs.text:
Cool Flames Investigation The objectives of this investigation are to:
    1) Examine the combustion behavior of n-dodecane and mixtures of n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at pressures ranging from 0.25 atm to 5 atm.
    2) Analyze the effects of helium dilution on cool flame behavior.
    3) Examine the behavior of combustion characteristics.
    4) Investigate the relationship between droplet size, pressure, and flame extinction, and (5) understand the consequence of soot formation during cool flame combustion. n-dodecane; n-dodecane / iso-dodecane mixtures single droplet Multi-User Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA), Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)

docs.title: BASS
docs.text:
Burning and Suppression of Solids The two main objectives for BASS are to:
    1.) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test#1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity. The relation between these can be investigated by observing flames burning for the longer times available in flight. Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including wake flames which have characteristics of a fire burning behind another object (for example, a fire burning in tight area which may not be easily accessible).
    2.) Assess the effectiveness of an inert, gaseous extinguishing agent (similar to that used on ISS) in putting out flames over different materials, geometries, preheating, and flow. PMMA; SIBAL (cotton/fibreglass); Nomex blend; wax candle flat samples, 1 and 2 cm spheres, candles Microgravity Science Glovebox

docs.title: BASS-II
docs.text:
Burning and Suppression of Solids - II BASS-II results contribute to the combustion computational models used in the design of fire detection and suppression systems in microgravity and on Earth.
Objectives Include:
  1) Study the ignition, flame growth, flame spread, and extinction limits for solid fuels burning in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
  2) Begin to bridge the gap between the normal gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test #1 method, ground-based microgravity tests, and actual material flammability in microgravity.
  3) Provide SoFIE PIs with preliminary data to refine Science Requirements.
  4)  Practical, realistic (thicker) fuels in typical geometries will be examined, including slabs, cylinders, and spherical sections.

The primary variables include:
     • Forced flow velocity (speed and direction)
     • Ambient oxygen concentration (via working volume nitrogen vitiation)
     • Sample geometry (rods, spherical section, slabs, films, and fabric sheets PMMA (films, slabs, rods); SIBAL (cotton/fibreglass); Nomex; wax candle films 0.1 to 0.4 mm, slabs 1 to 5 mm, rods 6.35 to 12.7 mm diameter, fabric 1.2 or 2.2 cm wide Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)

docs.title: SPICE
docs.text:
Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment The objective of SPICE is to better understand the complex process of combustion by observing flames in a microgravity environment aboard the International Space Station (ISS) and analogous ground experiments.

Specific objectives were:
(1) Identify the laminar smoke-point properties of non-buoyant jet diffusion flames under various co-flow conditions in microgravity.
(2) Determine the effects of burner diameter and co-flow velocity on the luminous flame lengths and smoke points.
(3) Quantify the sooting propensity of different fuels, such as ethylene, propane, and propylene mixtures.
(4) Validate the correlation between luminous flame shape and residence time under microgravity conditions.
(5) Investigate the impact of air and fuel flow rate variations on smoke point phenomena in space. propylene; propane; ethylene; methane gas-jet flame in coflow, 1.6 mm nozzle (first PSI rows) Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG)

docs.title: SLICE
docs.text:
Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment Objective: The objective of this investigation is to better understand the structure and stability of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity.

Specific objectives of this investigation were:
1. To investigate the structure of laminar diffusion flames in microgravity to understand the stabilizing mechanisms at the flames base.
2. Determine the liftoff velocity limits for different fuels and burner diameters.
3. Evaluate the impact of fuel dilution with nitrogen on soot formation and flame stability.
4. Quantify the effects of microgravity on flame length and radiative heat loss compared to normal gravity conditions.
5. Validate numerical models for flame dynamics, soot production, and thermal radiation in non-premixed flames. methane; methane / nitrogen coflow jet flame

docs.title: SAME
docs.text: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment One of the major goals of this investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. A numerical code was to be developed to predict the smoke droplet growth as a function of the fuel pyrolysis rate, the thermodynamic properties of the pyrolysis vapor, and the flow environment. Teflon; Kapton; silicone rubber; cellulose lamp wick overheated (not burning) samples; smoke aged before measurement Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware
docs.source_ref: Urban et al., SAME Final Report (NIST, 5 Mar 2010), Table 1

docs.title: SAME-R
docs.text: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment-Reflight Similar to the original SAME investigation, the primary objective of the SAME-R investigation was to quantify the sizes that the liquid smoke particulate achieves in low gravity and to relate the droplet size distribution to the smoke generation and smoke transport conditions in the experiment. One of the problems encountered during the SAME investigation was that after the thermal precipitators were returned to the ground, it was found that all the TEM grids were severely contaminated with some unidentified foreign particles, making these grids unusable although some of them showed shapes of certain types of smoke particles. Based on that experience the SAME-R investigation employed several modification covering new materials, extended operating conditions, and diagnostic equipments. Kapton; silicone; lamp wick; Pyrell; Teflon overheated (not burning) samples; smoke aged before measurement Comparitive Soot Diagnostic Hardware; Refer to final report

docs.title: DAFT
docs.text:
Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2 The focus of DAFT / DAFT-2 was to mitigate the risk for the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME). SAME relied on a commercially available condensate nuclei counter, the TSI P-Trak,  to quantify smoke aerosols in a microgravity environment, however there were concerns that th P-Trak would not be reliable in microgravity as it relies on gravity to recycle isopropyl alcohol used in the measurement process.
DAFT / DAFT-2 tests that a modified P-Trak particulate counter would be accurate in microgravity.

Summarized objectives include:
    1) Demonstrate the Functionality of the Modified TSI P-Trak in Microgravity
    2) Compare the TSI P-Trak Performance against the DustTrak control
    3) Create and Analyze Aerosol Standards in Microgravity
    4) Ensure the reliability of future aerosol experiments test dust aerosol; cabin air particle counters sampling cabin air TSI P-Trak

docs.title: ACME-BRE
docs.text:
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments - Burning Rate Emulator The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties.
The specific flight objectives are as follows.
  1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2mixtures on porous circular burners of 25  and 50 mm diameter. Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures. NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen. Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.
  2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).
  3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits. ethylene, methane (pure or nitrogen-diluted), emulating solid and liquid fuels flat porous burner, 25 mm (some 50 mm) Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME

docs.text:
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame In order to provide the experimental data needed to allow rigorous testing of computational models at the extremes of the fuel dilution spectrum, we have the following objectives:
A) Characterize the behavior of weak coflow diffusion flames of methane and ethylene, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, lift-off heights, temperatures and extinction limits.
B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume fractions. methane; ethylene (nitrogen-diluted) coflow laminar jet flame Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME

docs.title: ACME-FlameDesign
docs.text:
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Flame Design The primary objectives of this flight experiment are:
A. Obtain soot-inception limits of quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames as functions of flow rate, Zst, amount of inert (N2 or CO2), and pressure for C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Obtain similar limits and temperatures for inverse and normal coflow flames.
B. Obtain detailed measurements in quasi-steady normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames for C2H4 and CH4. Determine the effects of flow rate, Zst, amount of N2, and pressure on flame temperature, size, color, and soot volume fraction. Evaluate the possible existence of steady flames.
C. Obtain extinction limits as functions of Zst, amount of N2, and pressure for normal and inverse spherical C2H4 and CH4 flames. Identify the corresponding temperatures in hot regions. Identify the presence of radiative or kinetic extinction. Evaluate whether pseudo-flammability limits can be obtained for these flames. ethylene; propane porous spherical burner; normal and inverse flames Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME), Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), Reconfiguration of Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR)

docs.title: ACME-sFlame
docs.text:
Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments-Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames A series of experiments is proposed with the following specific objectives, in both soot-free and sooty flames, to compare with detailed computational simulation to assess transport properties and detailed chemical kinetics (including chemiluminescence):
    Objective A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios   (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates.
    Objective B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).
    Objective C. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number. ethylene (nitrogen- or helium-diluted) porous spherical burner Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR), ACME

docs.title: PSI-117
docs.text: Effect of External Thermo-Convective Perturbation on Cool Flame Dynamics: A Multidimensional Multi-Physics CFD Analysis The objective of this ground investigation was to use flight data obtained from PSI through NASA’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) to quantify how externally imposed thermal and convective perturbations regulated the dynamics and ultimate fate of already established droplet cool flames, and to explain run-to-run variability by isolating the roles of deliberate heating and unintentional drift-induced convection. Focusing on both small and large droplets, the work mapped stability windows for ignition, sustained oscillation, transitions to hot ignition and warm-flame behavior, and extinction under microgravity. By leveraging and extending the FLEX data in the PSI, this study produced reusable models and sensitivity analyses that coupled low-temperature chemistry with transport and radiative effects.

docs.title: PSI-142
docs.text:
Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames By using the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) experimental data from the Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system of combustion science, the purpose of this grant was to conduct new simulations and ground-based experiments using ozone-sensitized counterflow flames to:
    1) Develop a new diagram of the flammability limits of diffusional cool flames affected by radiation, diffusion, and convection.
    2) Bridge the knowledge gap between the flammability limits and extinction limits of hot flames and cool flames.
    3) Verify the phenomena observed on the ISS flame extinguishment experiments.
    4) Obtain new, quantitative data of extinction limit, flame temperature, and species distribution for the validation of kinetic and radiation models involving cool flames.
    5) Extend the cool flame experiments from the original ISS droplet experiments to a more general ground-based combustion system involving radiation, diffusion, convection, and low-temperature chemistry while maintaining a one-dimensional geometry. counterflow flames (laboratory) Principal Investigator Laboratory Hardware

docs.title: PSI-60
docs.text: Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets This ground investigation  sought to increase understanding of the issues that control the large discrepancy between soot formation in 1g and in 0g flames.  The objective of this investigation was to integrate computational and experimental methods to derive temperature distributions and soot volume fractions from the Smoke Point in Coflow Experiment (SPICE) data available in PSI. By analyzing over 1600 raw DSLR images and incorporating advanced soot models, the study sought to improve understanding of soot formation, oxidation, radiative re-absorption, and aggregate growth in heavily sooting flames. The work further aimed to reconcile microgravity and normal gravity flame behavior, identify key physical and chemical processes influencing smoke point development, and provide a framework for evaluating model parameter sensitivity.

docs.title: PSI-62
docs.text:
Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity. Concurrent flame spread presented one of the greatest modeling challenges in combustion science due to the intricate coupling between heat transfer, mass transport, and chemical kinetics near the solid-vapor interface. Traditional modeling strategies often relied on hybridized turbulence and chemistry models that were not fully consistent and failed to capture important intermediate reaction pathways.
To overcome these shortcomings, this PSI grant advanced the use of an unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) framework that reduced the complexity of reacting systems by mapping them into lower-dimensional manifolds. The research aimed to leverage this methodology to simulate solid fuel combustion processes with high fidelity, using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks. Ultimately, the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials and to provide a tool that could also serve as a subgrid-scale model in large-eddy simulations of fires, supporting spacecraft safety and hazard mitigation.

docs.title: PSI-115
docs.text: Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity The objective of this investigation was to use numerical simulation to explore the influence of gravity on pyrolysis smoke growth from a fundamental perspective. The intention of this effort is to quantify the differences between microgravity and Earth gravity smoke, and to identify the fluid dynamic mechanisms that cause the differences.
